comparison: Both evaluations support the basic temperature preference findings (C1, C2). OpenEval focuses specifically on these two claims with detailed methodological assessment, while peer review groups them with broader taste-evoked findings (C3, C4, C7-C9). Both find the evidence solid and well-presented.

Strong overlap on taste vs. nutrient distinction claims (C3, C4, C7-C9). OpenEval evaluates C3-C10 as a comprehensive set demonstrating the two-component model, while peer review groups C1-C4, C7-C9 together. Both find the sucralose experiments convincing for separating taste from nutrient effects.

Both address sucralose properties and sweet taste importance (C5, C6, C10). OpenEval includes these within the broader taste vs. nutrient framework (C3-C10), while peer review treats them as foundational experimental design elements. Both accept these claims without challenge.

High agreement on genetic manipulation of sweet GRNs (C11-C13, C17-C18). OpenEval evaluates C11-C18 as converging evidence from multiple approaches, while peer review focuses on C11-C13, C17-C18. Both find the genetic evidence convincing for sweet GRN involvement.

Both support optogenetic activation findings (C14-C16). OpenEval includes these within the broader genetic manipulation framework (C11-C18), while peer review evaluates them separately. Both accept that optogenetic excitation of sweet GRNs drives warm preference.

Strong agreement on thermosensory neuron involvement (C22-C25, C64). Both evaluations support the findings but OpenEval explicitly notes a mechanistic gap in explaining why activating either warm or cold neurons produces the same directional effect. Peer review accepts the findings without noting this conceptual issue.

Both support olfactory involvement via Orco mutants (C26). OpenEval includes C76 (mammalian CPR context), while peer review focuses solely on C26. Peer review suggests better presentation by moving data to main figures, while OpenEval accepts the finding as clear.

Agreement on hunger signaling pathway involvement (C31, C32, C35, C38, C40). OpenEval evaluates a broader set (C29-C41, C62) including homology claims, while peer review focuses on key experimental findings. Both find the differential effects on taste-evoked vs. nutrient-induced responses convincing.

Both support clock gene involvement (C45, C46, C61). OpenEval evaluates C42-C47, C61 including feeding data complexities, while peer review focuses on C45, C46, C61. Both accept that clock genes control taste-evoked but not nutrient-induced warm preference.

Both address time-of-day experiments (C43, C44). OpenEval notes strain-specific differences and lack of clear linkage to feeding rhythms, while peer review accepts that taste-evoked warm preference occurs consistently despite rhythmic feeding patterns. Both support the findings.

Both address FLIC feeding data for clock mutants (C47). OpenEval notes the complex pattern with tim01 showing slightly higher glucose consumption, while peer review treats this as supporting data for clock gene phenotype without detailed analysis. Both accept the finding.

Both support the CPR framework and two-component model (C58-C60, C63). OpenEval explicitly flags C58, C77-C78 as speculative interpretations, while peer review enthusiastically endorses the CPR analogy as valuable for future research. Both find the conceptual framework well-supported.

Overlap on mammalian CPR background claims (C48-C57). OpenEval evaluates these as supporting the fly-mammal parallel with appropriate citations, while peer review treats them as established background facts. Both accept these claims without challenge.

Both support interpretive/mechanistic claims (C66, C77, C78, C95). OpenEval explicitly notes C77-C78 are speculative, while peer review accepts these interpretations within the endorsed CPR framework. Both find the functional interpretations reasonable.

Strong overlap on background literature claims (C67-C85). OpenEval evaluates these as contextual support from prior literature that frames current findings, while peer review treats them as established facts accepted without challenge. Both find all citations appropriate.

Overlap on mechanistic context claims (C86-C87, C89-C94). OpenEval evaluates these as supporting context with C88 noted as speculative, while peer review accepts them as established background. Both support these claims based on appropriate citations.

Both address the speculative explanation for fly food recovery (C88). OpenEval explicitly notes this remains speculative despite plausible fatty acid/amino acid sensing mechanism, while peer review accepts it within the CPR framework. Both support the interpretation.

Minimal overlap on thermosensory background (C19-C21). OpenEval includes these in the thermosensory neuron evaluation, while peer review treats them as established background facts. Both accept these claims.

Minimal overlap on C65 (warm/cold neuron involvement interpretation). OpenEval includes this in thermosensory findings, while peer review groups it with interpretive claims in CPR framework. Both support the claim.

Minimal overlap on C76 (mammalian CPR olfactory context). OpenEval includes this as supporting context for olfactory findings, while peer review treats it as established background. Both accept the claim.

Overlap on homology claims for hunger signaling pathways (C29-C30, C33-C34, C36-C37, C39, C41). OpenEval evaluates these as literature-supported homology claims within the hunger signaling analysis, while peer review treats them as established background facts. Both accept all claims.
Minimal overlap on C42 (clock gene background). OpenEval includes this in clock gene evaluation, while peer review treats it as established background. Both accept the claim.
